questions.q: What does DCSI stand for?
options: Decision Clarity System: Insurance
Damage Classification Standard: Insurance
Door Canvassing Sales Initiative
Dynamic Claims Settlement Index
questions.explanation: DCSI stands for Decision Clarity System: Insurance — CRC's proprietary framework for guiding homeowners through insurance-funded restoration using evidence, not pressure.

questions.q: What drives decisions in the DCSI framework?
options: Rep enthusiasm and urgency
Evidence and documentation
The homeowner's financial situation
Company revenue targets
questions.explanation: DCSI is built on evidence and documented findings — not pressure, emotion, or urgency tactics. The evidence speaks for itself.

questions.q: What is the rep's primary role under DCSI?
options: Closer and deal-maker
Pressure negotiator
Educator and evidence-based advisor
Contract coordinator
questions.explanation: Under DCSI, the rep is an educator and advisor. The homeowner makes the decision based on clear, documented evidence — not a sales pitch.

questions.q: Before a homeowner calls their insurance company, DCSI recommends they first:
options: Get three contractor bids
Have a professional inspection document the damage
Check if neighbors have filed claims
Call a public adjuster
questions.explanation: Getting a professional inspection documented before calling the carrier preserves evidence and prevents the carrier from minimizing or denying the claim.

questions.q: What separates DCSI from traditional roofing sales?
options: Faster closing timelines
Lower pricing strategy
The homeowner decides based on facts — reps never apply pressure
More aggressive follow-up sequences
questions.explanation: DCSI flips the traditional model — the rep presents evidence, and the homeowner arrives at their own decision through clarity, not persuasion.

questions.q: When a homeowner asks 'Should I file a claim?' the DCSI response is:
options: Yes, always file — you paid the premiums
That depends on your deductible
Show them the evidence and let them decide
File immediately before the storm date is too old
questions.explanation: DCSI never tells a homeowner whether to file. The rep shows documented evidence and empowers the homeowner to make an informed decision on their own.

questions.q: DCSI documentation of damage serves what primary purpose?
options: Satisfies CRC internal quality review
Creates undeniable evidence that drives the adjuster's findings
Protects the rep from liability
Speeds up the permit process
questions.explanation: Documented evidence — photos, test squares, soft metal, storm data — gives the adjuster no basis to minimize or deny a legitimate claim.

questions.q: Under DCSI, when does a rep discuss price with the homeowner?
options: At the door during the initial pitch
After the inspection but before the adjuster
Never before claim approval — price is determined by the carrier scope
During the adjuster meeting
questions.explanation: Price is a carrier determination, not a rep pitch. Discussing price before approval creates confusion and undermines the evidence-first model.

questions.q: What is the rep's job at the adjuster meeting under DCSI?
options: Negotiate the scope directly with the adjuster
Present documented evidence and let it lead the conversation
Stay in the background to avoid conflict
Bring the homeowner's insurance policy to review
questions.explanation: The rep's role is to present a documented, HAAG-standard inspection report. Evidence-first forces the adjuster to respond to facts, not debate the rep.

questions.q: DCSI's principle regarding partial approvals is:
options: A partial approval is better than no approval — take it
Partial approvals are not worth fighting
Every documented line of damage deserves full indemnification — supplement everything missed
Let the homeowner decide if they want to push back
questions.explanation: DCSI never accepts a partial approval without a supplement fight. Every line item backed by evidence deserves full payment — that is the homeowner's right under their policy.

questions.q: HAAG Engineering is considered the gold standard for:
options: Roofing material manufacturing
Forensic roof inspection and damage documentation
Insurance policy underwriting
Contractor licensing requirements
questions.explanation: HAAG Engineering is an independent forensic standard recognized by carriers, courts, and the industry as the authoritative methodology for storm damage documentation.

questions.q: What is a 'test square' in HAAG methodology?
options: A 5x5 foot area marked for photo documentation
A 10x10 foot (100 sq ft) area used to count and document storm hits
The section of roof closest to the ridge
Any area with visible damage from the ground
questions.explanation: A test square is a 10x10 foot (100 sq ft) area randomly selected on each slope. Counting hits per test square creates a quantifiable, defensible record of storm impact density.

questions.q: HAAG defines 'functional damage' as:
options: Any visible change in shingle appearance
Damage that is covered under a standard homeowner policy
Damage that shortens material lifespan or compromises its waterproofing function
Damage that exceeds 50% of the roof surface
questions.explanation: Functional damage has a physical impact — it either shortens the useful life of the material or creates water infiltration risk. Cosmetic damage only changes appearance without affecting function.

questions.q: How do you mark hail hits during a HAAG-standard inspection?
options: Take photos only — no marking required
Use a chalk circle around each impact point and count per test square
Use orange spray paint on each hit
Record GPS coordinates of each damaged area
questions.explanation: Chalk circles quantify each storm hit within the test square. The count per 100 sq ft gives the adjuster a defensible, documented density of impact — not a subjective estimate.

questions.q: What makes soft metal damage critical to document in a hail claim?
options: Soft metals are the most expensive items to replace
It provides proof of hail size and frequency that cannot be disputed
Insurance always pays for soft metals without documentation
Soft metals show the storm direction
questions.explanation: Gutters, AC fins, metal flashing, and vents hold permanent dents from hail impact. They provide irrefutable physical evidence of hail size and density at the specific property.

questions.q: Why do insurance carriers accept HAAG inspection findings?
options: HAAG is a government-mandated standard
HAAG Engineering is an independent forensic standard recognized in courts and industry
Carriers are required by Ohio law to accept HAAG reports
HAAG certifications are required for all contractors
questions.explanation: HAAG Engineering's methodology is court-recognized and industry-standard. Carriers cannot easily dispute findings from a HAAG-trained inspector the way they can challenge a contractor's informal opinion.

questions.q: What is 'cosmetic damage' per HAAG?
options: Any damage to metal components
Damage that affects appearance only, with no impact on function or lifespan
Damage visible from the street
Damage caused by falling debris
questions.explanation: Cosmetic damage — scuffs, minor marks, aesthetic changes — does not compromise the shingle's waterproofing or shorten its lifespan. Carriers often try to classify all damage as cosmetic to limit payouts.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence in a HAAG four-step inspection?
options: Photograph, estimate, document, report
Safety assessment, document conditions, identify storm damage, determine causation
Ground inspection, roof access, photo, report
Inspect, quote, present, close
questions.explanation: The HAAG four-step process: (1) safety assessment, (2) document existing conditions, (3) identify and classify storm damage, (4) determine causation. This sequence creates a defensible chain of evidence.

questions.q: The minimum documentation in a HAAG-standard report includes:
options: Contractor license number and estimate only
Photos, test square hit counts, soft metal evidence, storm correlation, and damage classification
Before-and-after photos and carrier policy number
Video walkthrough and voice narration
questions.explanation: A HAAG-standard report requires: photos with scale, chalk-marked test squares with hit counts, soft metal documentation, NOAA storm data corroboration, and damage type classification per HAAG definitions.

questions.q: The HAAG standard matters because it:
options: Qualifies reps for higher commission tiers
Transforms a subjective claim into an objective, evidence-based case carriers cannot easily dispute
Reduces the time needed to complete an inspection
Automatically approves the claim with most carriers
questions.explanation: A HAAG-standard report is objective, quantifiable, and forensically sound. It removes subjective debate and forces carriers to respond to documented evidence — dramatically improving claim outcomes.

questions.q: What is 'functional' hail damage to asphalt shingles?
options: Any visible dent or mark on the shingle surface
Damage that compromises waterproofing integrity or shortens material lifespan
Hail impact that removes more than 50% of granules from a single shingle
Damage visible from a two-story ladder
questions.explanation: Functional hail damage has a consequence — it either shortens the shingle's useful life or creates a pathway for water infiltration. This is the threshold for a legitimate insurance claim.

questions.q: The primary evidence of hail damage to asphalt shingles is:
options: Cracked ridge caps
Granule loss with exposed black mat (bruising)
Missing tabs on the north slope
Buckled decking visible from the attic
questions.explanation: Granule loss exposing the black asphalt mat — combined with mat fracturing (bruising) — is the standard indicator of functional hail damage. Granules protect the mat from UV; their loss accelerates failure.

questions.q: Why is soft metal damage important in a hail claim?
options: Soft metals are the highest cost line item in a scope
It provides irrefutable physical evidence of hail size and density at the property
Carriers require soft metal photos before reviewing any claim
Soft metals show the storm direction
questions.explanation: Gutters, AC fins, metal flashing, and aluminum vents hold permanent hail dents. Unlike shingles, soft metals cannot be disputed as 'cosmetic only' — the dent is physical proof of impact size and frequency.

questions.q: What hail size typically begins to cause functional damage to standard 3-tab shingles?
options: Any size hail causes functional damage
1 inch or larger
2 inches or larger
Only hail accompanied by wind above 60 mph
questions.explanation: 1 inch or larger hail (quarter-size) typically causes functional damage to standard 3-tab shingles. Older or lower-quality shingles can sustain functional damage from smaller hail depending on impact velocity.

questions.q: Granule loss matters to a claim because:
options: Granules increase the property resale value
Granules protect the asphalt mat from UV degradation; their loss accelerates shingle failure
Granule loss is required to trigger a full replacement under all policies
Insurance companies value granules as a separate line item
questions.explanation: Asphalt granules are the UV shield for the shingle. Once hail strips them and exposes the mat, UV oxidizes the asphalt rapidly — turning a 25-year shingle into a 5-year liability.

questions.q: A hail 'bruise' affects a shingle long-term by:
options: Causing immediate leaks through the shingle
Fracturing the asphalt mat, allowing moisture infiltration and accelerating weathering
Changing the shingle color, which voids the manufacturer warranty
Creating a soft spot that collapses under foot traffic
questions.explanation: A hail bruise fractures the fiberglass mat beneath the granules. Initially, the shingle may still shed water — but the fracture point becomes a crack over time, creating water infiltration risk.

questions.q: When photographing hail damage, your documentation must include:
options: Photos from the street showing the whole roof
Close-up with scale reference, chalk-circled test square, and soft metal evidence
Time-stamped photos from the day of the storm
Photos of the homeowner's insurance policy declarations page
questions.explanation: Three layers of documentation: (1) close-up with ruler/coin scale showing impact detail, (2) test square with chalk circles counting hits, (3) soft metal evidence confirming hail size. Together, these are unchallengeable.

questions.q: A carrier claims hail damage is 'cosmetic only.' Your evidence-based counter is:
options: Threaten to contact the state insurance commissioner
Show granule loss to exposed mat and fractured asphalt — functional damage per HAAG standards
Get a second inspector opinion
Ask the homeowner to reconsider filing
questions.explanation: Exposed mat + fractured asphalt = functional damage per the HAAG definition. The carrier's 'cosmetic only' classification is not defensible when the documentation shows mat exposure and bruising.

questions.q: Multiple hailstorms create what complication in a claim?
options: The latest storm automatically supersedes all prior damage
Attribution of damage to specific storm events — NOAA history is required
Carriers are not required to cover damage from multiple events
Multiple storms always result in automatic full replacement
questions.explanation: When multiple storms have hit a property, carriers will try to attribute damage to events outside the policy period. NOAA storm data for each date is required to isolate and document the correct insured event.

questions.q: When a carrier denies a hail claim citing 'normal wear and tear,' your strongest counter-documentation is:
options: The age of the roof from the original permit
NOAA storm data for the specific date + HAAG-documented impacts on soft metals
A second opinion from another roofer
The homeowner's original purchase documents showing roof condition
questions.explanation: Normal wear and tear does not create uniform dents on soft metals or granule loss in the specific pattern of hail impact. NOAA data plus HAAG soft metal documentation proves event causation, defeating the wear-and-tear argument.

questions.q: Wind damage to asphalt shingles is primarily identified by:
options: Missing shingles only — lifted shingles do not count
Creased, lifted, or torn tabs with compromised adhesion seals
Visible damage from the ground level
Storm direction matching the slope orientation
questions.explanation: Functional wind damage manifests as creased tabs (physical mat fracture), lifted corners (broken adhesive seal), and torn material — all of which compromise water resistance.

questions.q: When the adhesive seal between shingles fails due to wind, the result is:
options: Only cosmetic surface lifting that self-corrects in warm weather
Water infiltration risk from the open seal — functional damage
Voiding of the manufacturer warranty only
Disqualification from supplemental claims
questions.explanation: A broken adhesive seal creates a pathway for water to enter under the shingle during rain events. This is functional damage — not cosmetic — because it directly affects waterproofing integrity.

questions.q: What is 'racking' damage in a wind context?
options: Shingles being physically removed from the roof deck
Lateral displacement of shingles by wind force, breaking the factory adhesive bond
Damage to the roof rack above a garage
Ridge cap shingles detaching from the apex
questions.explanation: Racking occurs when wind force moves shingles sideways, breaking the adhesive bond that seals each course to the one below. The shingle may remain in place but is functionally compromised.

questions.q: How do you verify wind speed at a specific property address for a specific storm date?
options: Call the local TV weather station
NOAA storm data by ZIP code and date, corroborated by local weather station records
Check the homeowner's personal weather station data
Use the closest airport's ATIS recording
questions.explanation: NOAA maintains historical storm records searchable by ZIP code and date. This data provides the authoritative wind speed record that correlates your documented damage to a specific covered event.

questions.q: What is 'creasing' damage on a shingle and why does it matter?
options: Surface scratches from debris impact — cosmetic only
Physical bending of the shingle that cracks the mat, compromising waterproofing
Edge wear from improper installation
Adhesive squeeze-out visible at tab edges
questions.explanation: A creased shingle has been physically deformed past its flex tolerance. The fiberglass mat cracks at the crease point, creating a fracture that allows moisture infiltration — functional damage by definition.

questions.q: A carrier argues that lifted shingles 're-sealed in warm weather.' Your response is:
options: Agree and offer a reduced scope without lifted shingles
Re-sealing does not restore a broken seal — adhesive once fractured cannot fully re-bond
Ask for a joint inspection with both the carrier and manufacturer
Document that the carrier inspector failed to note the re-sealing
questions.explanation: Adhesive sealant that breaks under wind force does not return to factory strength when temperatures rise. A re-sealed shingle remains vulnerable — especially at the original failure point.

questions.q: The functional test for wind-creased shingles is:
options: Pull the shingle edge up and check if it springs back
Flex the crease area — a functionally damaged shingle will crack or show mat separation
Use a moisture meter on the shingle surface
Check for discoloration using UV light
questions.explanation: Flexing a creased shingle at the damage point reveals mat integrity. If the mat cracks or separates, the shingle is functionally compromised — it cannot waterproof under rain and freeze-thaw cycles.

questions.q: Under Ohio code, how many damaged shingles per slope typically trigger full replacement vs spot repair?
options: More than 5 shingles per slope
More than 10% of shingles on a slope — spot repair cannot match or comply aesthetically
Any visible wind damage requires full replacement automatically
Replacement is required only when all four slopes are damaged
questions.explanation: When more than 10% of a slope is damaged, spot repair creates a non-matching, non-code-compliant result. Ohio code and manufacturer warranty requirements support full slope replacement in these cases.

questions.q: What evidence combination is required to prove wind damage causation?
options: Homeowner testimony about the storm plus contractor photos
Creased/lifted shingles + adhesion failure documentation + NOAA wind speed data for the event date
Insurance claim number and contractor license only
Before-and-after aerial images from Google Maps
questions.explanation: Wind damage causation requires three elements: (1) documented physical damage to shingles, (2) NOAA-verified wind speeds at the property on the storm date, and (3) adhesion failure evidence showing storm impact, not wear.

questions.q: Why does 're-sealing' not fix wind crease damage?
options: Re-sealing increases the shingle's susceptibility to UV damage
The fiberglass mat is physically fractured — adhesive can seal the gap but cannot restore structural integrity
Manufacturer warranties do not cover re-sealed shingles
Re-sealing changes the shingle color and creates a mismatch
questions.explanation: A crease fractures the internal mat structure. Adhesive sealant addresses the gap at the surface level but cannot repair the microscopically cracked fiberglass beneath — the functional damage persists regardless of re-sealing.

questions.q: Ohio Residential Building Code requires drip edge at what locations?
options: At eaves (horizontal edges) only
At rakes (sloped edges) only
Both eaves AND rakes — per IRC Section R905.2.8
Only at valleys and penetrations
questions.explanation: IRC Section R905.2.8, adopted by Ohio, mandates drip edge at both eave edges (horizontal) and rake edges (sloped). Carriers frequently omit rake drip edge — cite the code explicitly when supplementing.

questions.q: Under Ohio code, what is the maximum number of shingle layers permitted on a residential roof?
options: Two layers maximum
Three layers if the deck is structurally sound
One layer — all previous shingles must be removed before new installation
No maximum if the deck passes inspection
questions.explanation: Ohio adopted the IRC requirement of one shingle layer maximum. Regardless of the existing shingle condition, a complete tear-off is required before new installation — and insurance must pay for it if a covered storm requires replacement.

questions.q: Ice and water shield is required by Ohio code in what area?
options: The entire roof surface for any claims after 2020
The first 24 inches past the interior wall line at the eave edge
Only at valleys and around penetrations
Anywhere the pitch is below 3:12
questions.explanation: Ohio code (IRC R905.2.7) requires ice and water shield to extend from the eave edge to a point at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line — ensuring protection at the critical freeze zone.

questions.q: What is a 'code upgrade' and why must insurance pay for it?
options: An optional upgrade the homeowner selects for better materials
A required improvement to bring replacement installation to current code — insurance must restore to code compliance
A GAF manufacturer warranty requirement
An upgrade that requires a separate rider on the homeowner policy
questions.explanation: When a covered loss requires replacement, the replacement must meet current code — even if the original installation was non-code. Most policies have a 'code upgrade' provision; carriers are obligated to pay for code-required improvements.

questions.q: GAF's Lifetime Roofing System warranty requires:
options: Any licensed contractor using at least 3 GAF products
All qualifying GAF components installed by a GAF Factory Certified Contractor, registered with GAF
Installation by a GAF master roofer with 10+ years experience
GAF shingles only — other components may be any brand
questions.explanation: The GAF Lifetime System warranty is conditional: all qualifying GAF components (shingles, underlayment, starter, ridge cap, ventilation) must be used, installed by a GAF Factory Certified Contractor, and registered within 45 days of completion.

questions.q: What is the required attic ventilation ratio under Ohio code?
options: 1:300 (1 sq ft per 300 sq ft of attic floor)
1:150 (1 sq ft net free ventilation per 150 sq ft of attic floor space)
1:100 for all Ohio climates
Ventilation is not code-specified in Ohio — builder discretion
questions.explanation: Ohio code follows the IRC standard of 1:150 — one square foot of net free ventilation area per 150 square feet of attic floor space. Proper ventilation is a manufacturer requirement for warranty validity.

questions.q: When a carrier omits drip edge from the settlement, you cite:
options: The original roofing contract showing drip edge was installed previously
IRC Section R905.2.8 mandating drip edge at both eaves and rakes — it is a code requirement, not an option
The manufacturer installation guide as your only authority
A neighborhood association requirement
questions.explanation: Drip edge at eaves AND rakes is not a contractor preference — it is a code requirement under IRC R905.2.8, adopted in Ohio. Insurance must cover the cost of code-mandated installation items.

questions.q: Starter strip at rakes is required by:
options: GAF manufacturer warranty only — not code
IRC building code AND most manufacturer warranties — both require it
Only when the existing starter strip is damaged
When the homeowner requests it as an upgrade
questions.explanation: Starter strip at rake edges is required by both code (IRC) and manufacturer installation specifications (including GAF). Carrier scopes that omit rake starter strip are incomplete and supplementable with citation to both authorities.

questions.q: GAF Factory Certified Contractor status requires:
options: Passing a written exam only — no installation verification
Training, demonstrated installation quality standards, and registration with GAF
Simply purchasing more than $50,000 of GAF product annually
A state roofing license and 5 years in business
questions.explanation: GAF Factory Certified status requires approved training, adherence to installation standards, and ongoing registration with GAF. It is not automatic with any purchase level — it is performance-based certification.

questions.q: Why does Ohio code require tear-off even when existing shingles appear structurally intact?
options: Tear-off costs are always covered by insurance regardless
Code prohibits more than one layer — adding over existing shingles violates code regardless of condition
GAF warranties require tear-off on all installs
Tear-off is required only when the deck has soft spots
questions.explanation: Ohio's adoption of the IRC one-layer maximum means: if you're replacing a roof, the existing shingles come off — period. Condition of the existing shingles is irrelevant. Insurance owes the tear-off cost as part of the covered replacement.

questions.q: The DCSI door approach opens with:
options: Your company name and a price estimate
A referral from a neighbor and a product brochure
Storm education and the homeowner's right to an inspection — not a sales pitch
A question about their current contractor relationship
questions.explanation: DCSI at the door starts with value: 'We've been inspecting roofs in your neighborhood after the storm and found significant damage. You have the right to a free inspection.' Lead with education, not your brand.

questions.q: When a homeowner says 'I don't want to raise my rates,' the evidence-based DCSI response is:
options: Explain you have a program to cover deductibles
In Ohio, a weather event claim cannot directly cause a rate increase — it is a non-fault covered loss
Agree that filing may affect rates and suggest alternatives
Promise that rates will not go up based on your experience
questions.explanation: Ohio insurance law limits carriers from raising rates specifically for non-fault weather events. The homeowner's concern is real but misplaced — educate them on this protection and restore their confidence.

questions.q: What is the purpose of walking the roof WITH the homeowner during the inspection?
options: To get their verbal approval of the damage before the adjuster arrives
Create shared conviction through shared evidence — they see what you see, eliminating doubt
To ensure they understand the full replacement cost before the claim
To have a witness for liability purposes during the inspection
questions.explanation: When a homeowner sees the damage with their own eyes — chalk circles, soft metal dents, exposed mat — they become a believer in the claim through evidence, not through a rep's pitch. Shared vision equals shared commitment.

questions.q: Under DCSI, when do you first discuss the price of the project?
options: At the door to build credibility
After the inspection but before the adjuster visit
Never before carrier approval — price is determined by the scope the carrier approves
During the adjuster meeting to reinforce the value
questions.explanation: Price is the carrier's output — their scope determines what gets replaced and at what price. Discussing price before approval creates confusion, pushback, and takes the rep out of the advisor role.

questions.q: Your role at the adjuster meeting under DCSI is:
options: Negotiate the scope directly — be aggressive
Let the adjuster work without interference to avoid conflict
Be present, lead with documented evidence, and let the evidence drive the adjuster's findings
Bring the homeowner to advocate for the claim themselves
questions.explanation: Reps who skip adjuster meetings get 30-40% less approved on average. Your job is to be present, show your HAAG documentation first, and guide the adjuster through the evidence — without arguing.

questions.q: When a homeowner objects 'I'll just use whoever the insurance company sends,' your response is:
options: Offer a lower price point to compete with the carrier's preferred contractor
Explain they have the legal right to choose their own contractor — and that your inspection protects their interests
Agree and hand them your card if they change their mind
Explain that preferred contractors take shortcuts to protect carrier costs
questions.explanation: Ohio law protects a homeowner's right to choose. Preferred contractor lists benefit the carrier, not the homeowner. Your job is to educate — not disparage the preferred contractor, but assert the homeowner's right clearly.

questions.q: What is the biggest mistake reps make at the door under DCSI?
options: Talking too much about storm damage technical details
Not bringing enough brochures
Pitching the company, product, or price before establishing the problem and the homeowner's rights
Skipping the soft metal documentation
questions.explanation: The moment you lead with 'Let me tell you about Columbus Roofing Company,' you're a salesperson. Lead with the storm, the damage, and the homeowner's rights — become an advisor before you become a contractor.

questions.q: After the adjuster meeting, what must the rep do immediately?
options: Order materials based on the adjuster's verbal scope
Begin scheduling the installation crew
Review the adjuster's written scope for every missing line item and begin supplement documentation
Send the homeowner a thank you card
questions.explanation: The adjuster's written scope is the starting point for negotiations — not the finish line. Review it line by line against your documented inspection before a single nail is driven.

questions.q: A signed Agreement to Inspect (ATI) accomplishes what?
options: Commits the homeowner to use CRC regardless of claim outcome
Grants the rep permission to inspect under CRC's documented protocol — no financial obligation to the homeowner
Gives CRC legal authority to contact the insurance company on behalf of the homeowner
Waives the homeowner's right to choose another contractor
questions.explanation: The ATI grants inspection permission only — it creates no financial obligation. It protects the homeowner by documenting that CRC's inspection is professional and protocol-based, not a casual visit.

questions.q: The strongest close in DCSI is:
options: A limited-time offer tied to the storm response window
A guarantee that the claim will be approved if they sign today
Presenting the evidence and allowing silence — let the homeowner reach their own conclusion
Asking three closing questions in sequence
questions.explanation: Pressure closes undermine DCSI credibility. After showing documented evidence, let silence work. A homeowner who decides on their own based on facts is a committed homeowner — not a closed deal that unravels.

questions.q: What is Xactimate?
options: CRC's internal pricing software
The industry-standard insurance estimating software used by all major carriers to build claim scopes
A HAAG Engineering documentation tool
An Ohio state insurance department reporting system
questions.explanation: Xactimate is the universal estimating platform. Every supplement, negotiation, and scope must be structured in Xactimate format — carriers will not respond to anything outside their workflow.

questions.q: What does 'ACV settlement' mean?
options: The carrier is paying the full replacement cost immediately
The carrier is paying only the depreciated value — recoverable depreciation is withheld until installation is proven
The claim was denied and ACV is the compromise amount
Ohio law requires ACV settlement for all roof claims under 5 years old
questions.explanation: ACV (Actual Cash Value) is the depreciated value — what the roof is worth today, not what it costs to replace. The carrier holds the recoverable depreciation until you submit proof that the work was actually completed.

questions.q: Recoverable depreciation is released when:
options: The homeowner signs the contract with the contractor
Within 30 days of claim filing by law
The carrier receives proof of completion — final invoice and completion photos
When the rep calls the carrier after installation
questions.explanation: Carriers hold recoverable depreciation until the replacement is confirmed complete. Submit: final invoice, job completion photos, and (with some carriers) a signed homeowner completion certificate.

questions.q: The most frequently missed line item in Ohio adjuster scopes is:
options: Ice and water shield at eaves
Starter strip at rakes — almost always omitted from original adjuster scopes
Ridge cap installation
Permit fees
questions.explanation: Rake starter strip is the #1 missed item statewide. Adjusters include eave starter but routinely skip rake starter — which is separately required by code and manufacturer specs. Always line-item it in every supplement.

questions.q: State Farm's most common tactic in Ohio claims is:
options: Deny the claim outright and require a re-inspection
Omit drip edge at rakes, undercount squares, and apply excessive depreciation — all three must be fought every time
Approve quickly at full scope to avoid litigation risk
Request independent inspection from their preferred contractor
questions.explanation: State Farm has a pattern in Ohio: missing drip edge at rakes, square footage undercount, and aggressive depreciation. Know these patterns going in and pre-prepare your supplement for all three on every State Farm claim.

questions.q: How do you structure a supplement for a carrier?
options: Send a revised contractor estimate with a cover letter
Line-by-line comparison: carrier scope vs corrected scope, with code citation and photo backup for every delta
Email the adjuster a list of missing items verbally
Have the homeowner call the carrier directly to request additional items
questions.explanation: A supplement must mirror Xactimate format: identify the carrier's scope line, add the missing or corrected line with the correct Xactimate code, cite the justification (code section or manufacturer spec), and attach supporting photos.

questions.q: When should a supplement be submitted?
options: After installation is complete and the carrier can see the full scope
As soon as you identify discrepancies — ideally before installation begins
Within 90 days of the original claim approval
Only when the carrier has sent the first ACV check
questions.explanation: Some carriers reject supplements after installation is complete. Document gaps, submit early, and get written response before starting work. Post-install supplements on denied items are much harder to win.

questions.q: What is a 'partial approval' and what is the correct response?
options: The carrier approves the claim but deducts the deductible — normal process
The carrier approves some items but denies others — respond with a written supplement citing code and HAAG documentation for every denied item
The homeowner declined some items to lower their deductible
Insurance approves only ACV on the first check — recoverable depreciation comes later
questions.explanation: A partial approval means the carrier pushed back on specific line items. Each denied item needs its own supplement response with: the Xactimate line, code citation, HAAG documentation, and photos. Never accept a denial without a documented fight.

questions.q: What is the carrier's obligation after receiving a supplement in Ohio?
options: Carriers have no defined timeline to respond to supplements
They must review and respond in writing — Ohio's standard is 15 business days for response
Carriers must approve supplements within 7 days or they are auto-approved
The supplement must be reviewed by the state insurance department before the carrier responds
questions.explanation: Ohio insurance regulations require timely response to claim-related communications. Standard practice is 15 business days. Document every submission with date-stamped copies so you have a paper trail if the carrier stalls.

questions.q: Your strongest supplement package always includes:
options: A contractor bid comparison showing market pricing
HAAG inspection report, NOAA storm data, code citations, and supporting photos — the trifecta no adjuster dismisses easily
A letter from the homeowner explaining why the damage is severe
An estimate from a competing contractor showing higher pricing
questions.explanation: The supplement trifecta: (1) HAAG documentation proving functional damage, (2) NOAA data confirming the covered storm event, (3) code citations making the line items mandatory. This combination creates a supplement carriers cannot responsibly deny.

questions.q: At what stage should color selection happen?
options: At the door during the initial inspection visit
After the rep believes damage is present but before the adjuster
After written claim approval and before material ordering — never before approval
During installation when the crew is on-site
questions.explanation: Color selection before approval creates a liability — the homeowner has made a commitment before knowing if the claim will be approved, at what scope, or with what material tier. Lock color after written approval only.

questions.q: What constitutes a complete job packet?
options: Signed contract plus a photo of the completed roof
Contract, approved insurance scope, color selection, permit (if required), certificate of insurance, and final invoice
Just the signed contract and homeowner ID
Insurance approval letter and material quote
questions.explanation: A complete job packet protects everyone: contract documents the agreement, scope documents what was approved, color documents the homeowner's selection, permit is code compliance, COI protects the homeowner, and final invoice triggers depreciation release.

questions.q: When is a building permit required for a roof replacement in Ohio?
options: Only when the roof is over 15 years old
Never — Ohio has no permit requirement for re-roofing
Most Ohio municipalities require a permit for full roof replacement — verify local requirements before every job
Only when a structural change is being made to the roof deck
questions.explanation: Permit requirements vary by municipality in Ohio. Failure to pull a required permit is a code violation that can create liability for the contractor and homeowner. Always verify before scheduling.

questions.q: When must a mortgage company endorse an insurance claim check?
options: Only for checks over $10,000
Whenever the mortgage company is named on the check — regardless of amount
Only when the homeowner requests it
When the loan-to-value ratio is above 80%
questions.explanation: If the insurance check is made payable to both the homeowner and the mortgage servicer, that servicer must endorse it — no exceptions. This is a legal requirement based on the servicer's insurable interest in the property.

questions.q: When should installation begin?
options: After the adjuster visit, once damage is documented
After written claim approval, signed contract, and color selection — never on verbal approval
As soon as the homeowner gives verbal permission
When materials are ordered and deposited
questions.explanation: Verbal approval means nothing in a claim dispute. Written approval documents what the carrier has agreed to pay. Signed contract documents what the homeowner agreed to. Color selection documents their choice. All three before the nail gun starts.

questions.q: How do you handle a two-party insurance check made out to both the homeowner and mortgage company?
options: The homeowner deposits it and pays the contractor from their account
Contact the mortgage servicer's loss draft department, submit required paperwork, and follow their disbursement process
The contractor deposits the check and handles the mortgage company separately
Endorse the check on behalf of the mortgage company with homeowner permission
questions.explanation: Mortgage servicers have loss draft departments specifically for this process. Submit: contractor license, COI, signed contract, scope, and completion documentation per their requirements. Each servicer has a slightly different process — learn them.

questions.q: What triggers the release of recoverable depreciation?
options: The homeowner calling the carrier to confirm satisfaction
Signing the contractor's completion certificate only
Final invoice, completion photos, and sometimes a signed completion certificate submitted to the carrier
Automatic release 90 days after ACV settlement
questions.explanation: Recoverable depreciation release requires proof that the work was actually done. Submit: final invoice matching the approved scope, post-installation photos, and homeowner-signed completion certificate if the carrier requires it.

questions.q: What must be submitted to release recoverable depreciation from a carrier?
options: A verbal update call to the adjuster
Final invoice plus completion photos — and sometimes a signed completion certificate per carrier requirements
The original signed contract showing the project price
A HAAG post-installation inspection report
questions.explanation: Every dollar of recoverable depreciation requires documented proof of completion. Keep photo documentation of the finished roof organized by scope section — ridge, eaves, penetrations — for each carrier's requirements.

questions.q: Xactimate pricing is localized using:
options: The national average for residential roofing
The contractor's historical pricing database
The property's ZIP code for market-specific labor and material pricing
The insurance company's internal pricing tables
questions.explanation: Xactimate uses ZIP code-based pricing that reflects local labor rates and material costs. A scope generated for Columbus, Ohio uses Columbus ZIP pricing — not a national average. Always verify the ZIP code in every scope.

questions.q: The job packet protects you most critically when:
options: You need to market CRC on social media
Disputes arise about what was approved, priced, or promised — documentation is your only defense
The GAF warranty registration is filed
The homeowner requests a timeline change
questions.explanation: Without a complete job packet, a dispute is a 'he said, she said' situation. With a complete packet, you have: what the carrier approved in writing, what the homeowner signed, what color they chose, and what you completed. Disputes resolve in your favor.

questions.q: Why should a homeowner call CRC before calling their insurance company after a storm?
options: CRC can file the claim faster than the homeowner can
An independent inspection documentes damage before the carrier can minimize or deny it
Insurance companies won't talk to homeowners directly — a contractor must call first
CRC handles all communication with the carrier on the homeowner's behalf
questions.explanation: Once the carrier sends their adjuster without prior documentation, the homeowner is negotiating from weakness. An independent inspection first creates documented evidence the carrier must respond to — not dismiss.

questions.q: What is a homeowner's legal right regarding contractor selection in Ohio?
options: The homeowner must use the carrier's preferred contractor for warranty coverage
The homeowner may choose from a short list the carrier provides
The homeowner has the right to choose any licensed contractor for approved insurance work — carriers cannot mandate specific contractors
Contractor choice is only unrestricted for jobs under $5,000
questions.explanation: Ohio law protects free contractor choice. Preferred contractor programs benefit the carrier — preferred contractors are trained to scope jobs at the carrier's target cost, not the homeowner's full entitlement.

questions.q: What is 'Replacement Cost Value' (RCV)?
options: The original cost of the roof when the home was purchased
What the used roof is worth on the open market today
The cost to replace damaged materials with like-kind and quality at today's prices, with no depreciation
The amount the carrier is willing to pay before negotiation
questions.explanation: RCV is the full cost to restore your roof to its pre-loss condition at today's labor and material costs. Most policies cover RCV — not what the old roof was worth, but what it costs to replace it properly today.

questions.q: What is 'Actual Cash Value' (ACV)?
options: The full replacement cost of the roof in today's market
The depreciated value — RCV minus depreciation withheld until repairs are complete
The appraised value of the home's roofing system by a licensed appraiser
The contractor's actual cost to complete the project
questions.explanation: ACV is the initial carrier payment — what the roof is worth after depreciation. If you have an RCV policy, the withheld depreciation (recoverable) is released after you submit proof of completed repairs.

questions.q: Filing a weather-related roof claim in Ohio should or should not raise your homeowner insurance premium?
options: Should raise premiums — any claim increases risk profile
Should not raise premiums — Ohio limits rate actions for non-fault weather events specifically
Always raises premiums by a set percentage under state law
Depends entirely on the carrier — no consistent rule in Ohio
questions.explanation: Ohio insurance regulations limit a carrier's ability to raise rates specifically due to weather-related claims — events outside the homeowner's control. Homeowner fear of rate increases is common and often unfounded for storm claims.

questions.q: What is 'recoverable depreciation' and when is it available?
options: Money the homeowner receives immediately as cash in hand
The difference between ACV and RCV — released by the carrier after proof of completed repairs
A bonus payment carriers provide for fast claim resolution
Depreciation the homeowner can claim on their tax return
questions.explanation: Recoverable depreciation is the gap between what the carrier initially pays (ACV) and what the full replacement costs (RCV). Submit proof of completion — final invoice plus photos — and the carrier releases the held amount.

questions.q: When an insurance company offers their preferred contractor, homeowners should:
options: Accept — preferred contractors have better pricing
Know they have the legal right to choose any licensed contractor — preferred lists benefit carriers, not homeowners
Always reject — preferred contractors do poor work
Ask the carrier to provide three options from their list
questions.explanation: Preferred contractor programs represent a conflict of interest. The contractor is incentivized to scope at the carrier's target cost. Homeowners who understand their rights and exercise free contractor choice consistently receive better outcomes.

questions.q: How long does a homeowner typically have to file a property claim in Ohio?
options: 30 days from the storm date
6 months from discovery of damage
Most policies allow 1-2 years; Ohio has a 2-year statute for property damage — but filing early strengthens the claim
No deadline — claims can be filed anytime during policy coverage period
questions.explanation: While most Ohio homeowner policies allow 1-2 years to file, waiting weakens your claim — storm attribution becomes harder, damage worsens, and NOAA data correlation ages. File with documented evidence as soon as damage is confirmed.

questions.q: What is a public adjuster?
options: An employee of the insurance company who handles large commercial claims
A licensed professional who represents the homeowner in insurance claims — for a percentage of the settlement
A state government official who mediates disputed claims
A contractor who also holds an insurance adjuster license
questions.explanation: A public adjuster is a licensed professional who advocates for the homeowner in complex or disputed claims — working independently from the carrier. They charge a percentage of the settlement (typically 10-15%) and are most valuable in high-dollar disputed claims.

questions.q: A homeowner's strongest protection in any disputed insurance claim is:
options: Hiring an attorney to write a demand letter immediately
Threatening the carrier with a complaint to the Ohio Department of Insurance
A fully documented, HAAG-standard inspection report with photos, measurements, and code citations
Having the most neighbors file the same claim simultaneously
questions.explanation: Documentation is the homeowner's armor. A HAAG-standard inspection report — with test squares, soft metal evidence, NOAA correlation, and code citations — is the most effective tool in any disputed claim. It is objective, forensic, and legally defensible.
